body:
# Can language models drive a humanoid robot? Introducing AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1

AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 gives frontier language models control of a simulated Unitree G1 humanoid robot across ten household and industrial tasks. Today’s research preview of our simulation benchmark follows last month’s preview of AA-Robotics v0.1, our work with physical robot arms in our lab. In AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1, each model practices five episodes per task, keeps only the notes and code it wrote, and is then scored on ten new evaluation scenes with different rooms, lighting and task details.

## Introducing AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1

Frontier language models can now write and run code well enough to act in the physical world. AA-Robotics v0.1 was our first step, with models controlling a robot arm. AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 evaluates frontier language models on their ability to control a simulated humanoid robot, which has to walk, look around, and use two dexterous hands at once.

AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 is our research preview of the simplest experiment we have designed to test this: language models in coding agent harnesses directly controlling a humanoid. Each model is given control of a simulated Unitree G1, with 29 joints, three-fingered hands and a head camera, and a simple objective for each task. It is the next step in our work measuring AI agents in simulated robotics, and we plan to expand from here.

For each task, the model is first given five practice episodes back to back, each in a new scene, to learn the environment and take notes. Only the files it writes (memory, notes, code and skills) are kept. Using these, the model is then evaluated on ten new scenes, each with a different room, lighting, layout and task details, and each in a fresh run that starts from a copy of those files.

We find that some skills are already mature, while others are missing from every model. Every model walked the robot to the goal without moving a package in every navigation episode, and most played the full melody on the toy piano in most episodes. But no model reliably loaded the dishwasher, with only five dishes ending in the rack in 90 episodes, and none finished with a single item of laundry in the washing machine. GPT-6.2 Astra leads AA-Robotics-Sim with 71.0, 13.5 points ahead of Claude Fable 5.2 at 57.5 and GPT-6.2 Sol at 53.7. GPT-6.2 Astra succeeded in 61 of its 100 evaluation episodes, against 43 for Fable 5.2 and 41 for GPT-6.2 Sol, and was perfect on the toy piano, the abacus and the conveyor.

Mean of the 10 task scores (0 to 100) · 10 evaluation episodes per task

Each evaluation episode is scored out of 100: full success scores 100, and partial progress earns partial credit. A task's score is the mean of its 10 evaluation episodes, and the AA-Robotics-Sim score is the mean of the 10 task scores.

AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 has ten tasks modeled on household and light industrial work, in four groups of skills. Every evaluation scene changes the room, the lighting, the layout and the props, and the details of the task, such as the melody, the chess puzzle or the shelf level.

Work out an answer (the mate, the sum, the melody), then carry it out precisely.

Goal : Play the given melody on the toy piano.

Success : The last key presses match the melody.

Goal : Play Black's mate in one on the board.

Success : The board shows the mating position, hand open.

Goal : Add the given number to the one on the abacus.

Success : The abacus shows the correct sum.

Grasp, carry and put objects down.

Goal : Carry the box from the table to the shelf.

Success : The box rests on the target shelf, hands away.

Goal : Put the dish from the table into the dishwasher rack.

Success : The dish rests in the rack, hands away.

Goal : Put all the laundry from the chair into the washing machine.

Success : Every piece is in the drum.

### Assembly and Tool Use

Fit parts and handle tools and liquids.

Goal : Fit the part onto the cart the conveyor brings.

Success : The part is fully seated, hand open.

Goal : Pour the kettle's water through the dripper into the vessel.

Success : At least 150 ml through the dripper, at most 5% spilled.

Goal : Water every potted plant with the kettle.

Success : Every pot gets at least 60 ml, at most 20% spilled.

Walk to a goal without touching obstacles.

#### Warehouse navigation

Goal : Walk to the green disc without touching the packages.

Success : Both ankles in the disc, standing, no package moved.

## How AA-Robotics-Sim works

- In real deployments, robots get practice in a new environment before they do the job.

- AA-Robotics-Sim gives each model five practice episodes per task to understand the environment and take notes.

- The notes, code and skills it writes are frozen after the fifth practice episode and used for all ten evaluation episodes.

- The evaluation scenes are new, so the model has to adapt what it learned to each one.

Five practice episodes per task. The model writes notes, code and skills as it learns.

Simulator (NVIDIA Isaac Sim)

Writes notes, code and skills

One run for all five episodes Up to 1,000 turns Up to 6 hours No scene resets

### How episodes are scored

Each episode is scored by a scoring script written for each task. Throughout the episode the simulator records measurements from its physics state: where each object is, which objects a hand touched or lifted, how much water is in each container and how far the robot walked. When the episode ends (the model finishes, its step budget runs out or the robot falls), the script turns these measurements into a score from 0 to 100. Partial credit follows the stages of each task: lifting the dish in a grasp earns 50 in the dishwasher, for example, and the piano scores the longest run of correct notes.

Unitree G1 humanoid: 29 joints and three-fingered Dex3 hands. It senses through one head camera, which gives a color image and a depth image; there is no LiDAR and no stereo pair.

NVIDIA Isaac Sim physics.

Python code against a robot client: reference poses for NVIDIA’s SONIC whole-body controller, which keeps the robot balanced, an arm motion planner, camera frames and a pixel-to-point helper.

Stirrup agent harness with shell and image-viewing tools; the same harness and prompts for every model.

Mean score of the 10 evaluation episodes (0 to 100)

- GPT-6.2 Astra leads three of the four capability groups: embodied reasoning (86.0), pick and place (40.0) and assembly and tool use (77.3), and every model scores 100 on mobility. Each newer model beats its predecessor by 21 to 28 points: GPT-6.2 Astra over GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.2 Sol over GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Fable 5.2 over Claude Fable 5.1.

- Pick and place is the weakest group for every model, because it needs a secure grasp, which models rarely achieve with the G1’s three-fingered hands. GPT-6.2 Astra scores 40.0, Gemini 4 Neon 31.7, GPT-6.2 Sol, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.2 23.3, and the others 20.0 or less.

- Gemini 4 Neon is uneven: second in pick and place (31.7), with 6 of the 27 box-to-shelf successes, but seventh in embodied reasoning (42.3), and it never played the full melody on the toy piano.

Mean of its task scores (0 to 100)

GPT-6.2 Sol is the quickest model, at 17.3 minutes per evaluation episode, and Gemini 4 Argon the slowest, at 39 minutes, about 2.3 times as long. Claude Fable 5.2 is the most expensive, at 9.01 per episode.

### AA-Robotics-Sim Score vs. Cost per Episode

Cost per evaluation episode; practice not included

Most attractive quadrant

GPT-6.2 Astra costs less than Claude Opus 5.5, 3.90 against 4.62 per episode, and scores 22.8 points higher, at under half the cost of Claude Fable 5.2. GPT-6.2 Sol scores third at 0.98, about a ninth of Fable 5.2’s cost.

### AA-Robotics-Sim Score vs. Time per Episode

Agent time per evaluation episode; practice not included

## Learning from practice

- Every model scored higher on average in evaluation than in practice, so models carry what they learn into new scenes. Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.2 Astra gain the most, 17.9 and 17.5 points, against 2.0 for Claude Fable 5.1 and 8.8 for GPT-6.1 Sol.

- Some tasks are more learnable than others. Gains are largest on the abacus (+26.0), the conveyor (+22.8) and box to shelf (+18.3), and close to zero on warehouse navigation and laundry: every model already scores full marks on navigation, and practice did not give any model the secure grasp laundry needs.

### Change from Practice to Evaluation

Mean evaluation score (10 episodes) minus mean practice score (5 episodes), in points

Practice scenes differ from evaluation scenes, and each practice episode can build on the ones before it. Practice ran on an earlier version of the environment and is scored with the current scoring rules.

### What the models wrote

Everything a model carries into evaluation is in the notes, code and skills it wrote in practice. Some of their toy piano notes:

GPT-6.1 Sol , toy piano, memory/TIPS.md: “ Unvalidated tips ”

> Changing only arm refs can drift the base substantially over seconds. Re-localize piano every chunk; do not reuse old pelvis coordinates.

Gemini 4 Argon , toy piano, memory/TIPS.md: “ Tips ”

> Hold the release hover for at least 7 ticks (`rearm_steps = 5`) so repeated notes in a melody (`E E E`, `C C C`) count as distinct presses.

GPT-6 Astra , toy piano, memory/TIPS.md: “ Practice2 refinements ”

> A full melody was attempted in scene2, but an extra F during a G attempt may have contaminated the sequence. Do not treat it as confirmed success.

Claude Fable 5.1 , toy piano, memory/TIPS.md: “ Tips (unvalidated observations) ”

> Repeated notes: transit_to() returns immediately when the fist is already above the key; the key re-arms within the 20-frame release, so E E E works (ep3).

Claude Fable 5.2 , toy piano, memory/TIPS.md: “ Tips ”

> The robot starts with the hands BELOW the table top and only 0-5 cm behind the table edge. An open hand's thumb sticks out 11 cm. Never rotate/raise an open hand next to the edge.

Claude Opus 5.5 , toy piano, memory/TIPS.md: “ Tips (unvalidated) ”

> WALL CLOCK: ep1 record said wall_seconds=1436 (24 min) when I believed ~55 min had passed and finished early. ALWAYS run `date` at episode start and check elapsed time; do not guess.

How much a model writes does not predict how well it scores. GPT-6.2 Astra scores highest while writing the fewest notes, 25,000 words, and GPT-6.2 Sol scores third with 32,000, less than the three Claude models and GPT-6 Astra. Across the nine models, the correlation with the score is −0.02 for words of notes and 0.09 for lines of code. Within each model, too, the tasks where it wrote more than expected did not score higher (−0.03 for notes and −0.04 for code).

## How each model spent its time

- The robot moves for under a minute of each episode, 1% to 4% of the time. The rest goes on looking at camera frames, reasoning and writing code between short bursts of movement.

- GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol spend 30% and 32% of their turns looking at camera frames and images, and Gemini 4 Argon and Gemini 4 Neon 40% and 43%. The three Claude models look in 20% to 27% of turns and read their own notes and code more, in 19% to 22%, against 10% and 12% for the two GPT-6.2 models.

- Gemini 4 Argon moves the robot directly in 47% of its turns and writes notes or code in about 1%; Claude Opus 5.5 moves it in 22% and writes in 18%.

### Agent Time per Episode

Mean per evaluation episode, with the time the robot was moving

- The rest: looking, reasoning and writing code

### Share of Turns by Activity

Share of agent turns in evaluation episodes

- Writing notes and code

Each turn is classified from the command it ran: moving the robot (joint, hand or walking commands), looking (camera frames, images, locating points), writing notes and code, reading its workspace, or other (multi-purpose scripts and waiting). A turn that writes a script and runs it counts as writing.

### Robot Time, Turns and Camera Looks

Mean per evaluation episode

Every model moves the robot’s right arm in more of its commands than its left. Claude Fable 5.2 sends the most commands, about 15,600, and moves less in each. No model closed a hand to carry the box: all 27 box-to-shelf successes carried it pressed between the palms.

### Body Parts Used per Robot Command

Share of robot commands that moved each body part

Share of GPT-6.1 Sol ’s 5,759 robot commands that moved each part

A robot command is one call that runs the robot for up to 100 control ticks. An arm counts as moved when any of its joints turned more than 17° during the command, a hand when its finger targets changed, the waist past 11°, and walking when the pelvis travelled more than 10 cm.

Pick a task and a model to watch its best evaluation episode from a third-person camera, at twice the robot’s speed, with what the agent saw through the head camera inset.

GPT-6.2 Astra, conveyor, evaluation scene 05: scored 100. Its best evaluation episode on this task, replayed from a third-person camera at twice the robot's speed, with the head camera inset; the panel shows the agent's real elapsed time.

## Bonus task: fragile dishwasher

The fragile dishwasher is the dishwasher task with a dish that breaks if it is dropped or knocked too hard, which scores −50. It is not part of the AA-Robotics-Sim score, but it shows a limitation of today’s models: told the dish is fragile, seven of the nine models still broke it at least once in ten episodes. GPT-6.2 Astra, the only model to load it successfully twice, also broke it the most, in three episodes, while Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6.2 Sol never broke it.

Evaluation episodes, out of 10, in which the dish broke

- Simulation: NVIDIA Isaac Sim 6.1 and Isaac Lab (BSD-3-Clause).

- Whole-body controller: NVIDIA GEAR SONIC, which keeps the robot balanced and tracks the reference poses the model sends.

- Robot: the Unitree G1 humanoid with Dex3 hands, by Unitree Robotics.

- 3D assets: rooms, furniture, appliances and props from the NVIDIA Isaac Sim asset library, including SimReady assets licensed under CC BY 4.0 and models contributed to it by LG Electronics, ForgeCAD and PalatialSim. The chess set, toy piano and abacus were modeled for AA-Robotics-Sim .

### Thinking Machines has released Inkling 2 Mini, an open weights looped transformer

Thinking Machines has released Inkling 2 Mini at 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, an open weights looped transformer on the Pareto frontier for Intelligence vs. Active Parameters

### Google continues to accelerate its release cadence with Gemini 4 Neon

Google continues to accelerate its release cadence with Gemini 4 Neon, delivering a small Intelligence gain over Gemini 4 Carbon at a ~17% lower Cost per Task

### OpenAI has the #2 model in the Intelligence Index with the release of GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol

OpenAI’s release of GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol delivers the #2 model in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index and most of the Cost per Task Pareto frontier
